newsitem.title: USA: Clinton troubled by Mexico drug corruption case.
newsitem.headline: Clinton troubled by Mexico drug corruption case.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday called the alleged corruption of Mexico's drug czar "deeply troubling," and the White House said it had bluntly conveyed that message to Mexico's foreign minister.

Clinton said the Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo case would be a "mixed factor" in his pending decision on whether Mexico is cooperating in the anti-drug fight. U.S. trade and economic sanctions would flow from a negative decision.

The Mexican government announced on Tuesday that Gutierrez had been ousted as head of Mexico's National Institute for the Combat of Drugs (INCD) because of alleged links to a powerful narcotics trafficker, and charged with drug corruption.
"It's a very serious revelation and deeply troubling," Clinton told reporters after an unrelated White House event.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry later said visiting Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria had been given "several pieces of our mind" about the development when he met presidential adviser Thomas "Mack" McLarty and other U.S. officials on Thursday.
"The United States government in very stiff terms described our unhappiness and our concern about corruption apparently reaching such high levels in the Mexican government," McCurry said.
Despite the flap, a State Department spokesman said Washington would continue its close cooperation with Mexico on antinarcotics issues.
"It is absolutely in our interest as a nation to cooperate where we can with those it makes sense to cooperate with to get at this problem of narcotics trafficking," Davies said.
"So we're not going to suspend cooperation with the government of Mexico. That would be foolish of us," he added.
Clinton said he was encouraged by Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo's sacking of Gutierrez.
"They're obviously saying to the world and the people of Mexico, we will not tolerate the corruption if we find it and root it out, even if it's at the highest level," he said.
"They have not fooled around with this," Clinton added.
Clinton is to visit Mexico for talks with Zedillo April 11-12, and he said the anti-drug programme would be "at the top of our agenda."

He has to grade Mexico and 31 other countries at the end of the month in the "certification" process, Washington's annual evaluation of other governments' fight against drugs. Countries that fail that test may be subjected to U.S. economic and trade sanctions.

The United States has always certified its Latin American neighbour and third largest trade partner, despite evidence of high-level corruption and the fact that most drugs enter its territory through the 2,000-mile U.S.-Mexican border.
However, Democrat Clinton has been under fire from Republicans who say he has been too soft on Mexico.

Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican and chairman of the International Narcotics Control Caucus in Congress, said this latest incident raised serious questions about Mexico's reliability in the war against drugs.

At her weekly Justice Department news briefing, Attorney General Janet Reno said the Clinton administration was trying to determine whether Gutierrez had passed along sensitive U.S. information to drug dealers.

The New York Times reported on Thursday that Gutierrez had been privy to Mexico's most secret anti-drug operations and had received a classified briefing on U.S. operations during a visit to Washington last month.

"We are taking steps to review all of those issues and to take appropriate action," she said when asked if the administration would conduct a damage assessment on what information may have been compromised.

Reno, who met with Gutierrez and the new Mexican attorney general on January 28, acknowledged she was disappointed that he had been arrested, but still maintained she was "very impressed" by the Mexican government's quick action.

Reno said she had not received any advance word that he would be arrested. Asked about possible concern that U.S. intelligence agencies had been unaware of his background and the fact that he had recently moved into an apartment made available by an employee of a drug trafficker, Reno said, "All of those issues would be addressed."
